entry.title: fix(subtitles): key anchors by event, normalize the probed text, reme…
entry.content:
fix(subtitles): key anchors by event, normalize the probed text, remember failures

Second review pass. None of the three fires through today's producer, and each
is inside a contract the package already states.

The offset was looked up by token index alone. `_validate_palette` requires only
the (event, index) PAIR to be unique, so two events in one frame both answer to
index 0 — a frame with two events routinely has two first tokens — and the last
one measured hands its correction to the other word. Keyed by both now.

`_token_surface` sliced the raw text while every offset in that module is
defined against the normalized form (`\r` dropped, literal `\N` folded to one
newline). Past a break, every token read one character late and probed a
neighbour's string.

A probe that measures nothing is not retried forever. `extract_token_geometry`
refuses a palette colour that drew nothing, so one inkless token — text the
overprint would refuse anyway — fails the whole batch; with nothing recording
the attempt, the batch re-rendered once per geometry render for the session.

Smaller, from the same pass: the probe renders under the cue's own style, since
hinting and blur change a glyph's extent and measuring without them returns an
offset for a render nobody performs; at timestamp 0, since its events start
there and a long file would silently draw nothing; probe renderers evict
most-recently-used last like the cue's; and the row pitch is imported rather
than restated beside the frame it has to agree with.

`fragments`' docstring claimed extent-based routing to the raster device. That
is not implemented — `Fragment.matches` exists so the decision has a measurement
to stand on, and the docstring now says which of the two it is.

The first of these had a test that could not fail: it gave the two events
different token indices, so index-only keying passed it. Planting the defect is
what showed that, not reading it.

entry.title: fix(subtitles): bound the anchor cache and cover the probe wiring
entry.content:
fix(subtitles): bound the anchor cache and cover the probe wiring

Review findings on the anchor fix, both real.

The cache was unbounded, and its key is not stable the way its docstring
claimed. The size in it is the FRAME's, not the document's — `_palette_in_frame
_units` multiplies by `frame_height / play_res_y` — so dragging a window edge
mints a distinct float per pixel of height, every one of them a miss, every miss
a second libass render, and none of it ever reclaimed. "A repeated cue costs a
dict lookup" holds while the window is still and nowhere else. Now LRU, bounded,
and the comment says which case the bound is for.

The wiring had no coverage outside the `live` tier, which does not run in CI. A
wrong sign, a key that never matches, or a probe failing forever would all have
shipped green: the unit tests covered the pure arithmetic in `fragments` and
nothing that decides whether it is reached. Six tests over the backend probe —
offset carried, unprobed token left alone, measured once per cue, the cue's
renderer never pointed at a probe document, probe renderers closed, cache
bounded — and two over the subtraction itself in `test_overprint`.

Writing them exposed a fake that answered the cue's palette whatever document it
was handed, which made the probe's own colours unrecoverable and hid the whole
path behind the swallowed exception below. It answers the document now.

That exception no longer swallows silently: the first failure logs at warning,
since a probe that never succeeds disables the correction for the session with
nothing on screen to show it, and the rest stay at debug so a bad face cannot
flood the log.

entry.title: fix(subtitles): anchor the overprint where the token's ink actually l…
entry.content:
fix(subtitles): anchor the overprint where the token's ink actually lands

`\an7` positions the line box; a measured box is ink. Passing the ink origin to
`\pos` planted every redraw an ascent-gap low — 39% of the colour on the glyphs,
the rest on empty frame, with mpv's own subtitle showing through above it.

The offset cannot be derived from the box (libass reports no baseline) and is
not a constant: it depends on the token's tallest glyph, so it differs per word
in the same cue. It is measured instead, by rendering the fragmented layout the
overprint will ask for through the renderer that produced the boxes, and reading
where each token's ink lands.

    39% -> 99.9% of the overprint on a glyph mpv drew

Cost is one probe render per unseen (text, face, size). A repeated cue, a redraw,
and a recurring word all cost a dict lookup; a session's second and third render
of the same cue probe nothing. The probe uses its own renderer per font
environment so it never evicts the cue document from the renderer drawing the
cue, and a probe that fails leaves the offsets unrecorded — every redraw keeps
the origin it had before, which is today's behaviour.

The live oracle now drives `overprint_payload` rather than assembling paints
itself: the placement under test is a decision `_assign_rung` makes, and a test
that re-implements it would have kept passing while the shipped path was wrong.
That is not hypothetical — this commit's first two attempts passed the anchor
through a palette that dropped the text and through a field order that put
`coverage` into `anchor_dx`, and only the end-to-end pixel count caught either.

entry.title: chore(gate-d): make the geometry matrix report why a cell failed
entry.content:
chore(gate-d): make the geometry matrix report why a cell failed

A failing cell reported every criterion in its assessment as green, beside
`passed: false`. Nothing was wrong with either: `passed` is overwritten after
the mask comparison by four more criteria — the unsafe low-delta total, its
largest component, and nine render-input checks — and none of them is
serialized. So the number that decided the run was not in the run's own report,
and each investigation started by re-deriving it.

On a real macOS failure the answer turns out to be three pixels of slack:

    unsafe-low-delta-pixels 67 > 64
    unsafe-low-delta-component 34 > 23

with mask IoU 0.9609 against a 0.95 floor, bounds equal, and every input check
passing. `rejected_by` now carries that, quantified, per cell.

`sub-add` gets the same treatment for the other fault this job produces.
`cmd_track_add` (mpv, player/command.c) answers "error running command" for both
of its failure paths — playback already stopping, and the file not opening — so
the reply alone cannot tell them apart. mpv's log can, and the session already
keeps one; the constructor above reads it on the IPC path and this did not.

No threshold moves here. The 67-vs-64 and 34-vs-23 overshoot is a real
disagreement on one interaction (wrapping under a wide pixel aspect) and wants
its own look, which is easier now that the run says so itself.

entry.title: test(subtitles): measure whether the overprint colours the glyphs
entry.content:
test(subtitles): measure whether the overprint colours the glyphs

The boxes are hit targets, and the existing differential proves they are good
ones: a rectangle over a word, within a pixel of mpv's ink. The overprint asks a
second thing of the same rectangle — that redrawing the token there reproduces
the glyphs mpv drew — and nothing checked it. The two are not the same claim,
and only the first was true.

Measured by rendering the cue, then the cue plus our overprint events, through
one renderer, and asking what share of the colour landed on a glyph:

    39% on the glyphs, 916 coloured pixels on empty frame

`\an7` anchors the line box; the measured rectangle is ink. Handing the ink
origin to `\pos` plants the redraw an ascent-gap low — ~6px at fs40, growing
with the cue. Production agrees: its own drift log reads t=+14 b=+27 at
fs89.775 and t=+28 b=+37 at fs144.9, left ≈ 0 throughout, which is a
translation and nothing else.

Nobody sees it because the calibration catches it every time and demotes to the
raster device (`demotions[reason=measured-layout-drift]` in a real report). The
colour is correct; the fast path has been dead, disabled by a detector that
attributes our anchoring to the OSD library's font reach.

`fragments` measures the correction with the renderer that produced the boxes:
render the fragmented layout the overprint will ask for, read where each token's
ink lands, subtract. Applying it takes the same cue from 39% to 99.9%. It also
answers the second question — a token whose extent changes when drawn alone
cannot be redrawn faithfully and belongs on the raster device — which no
positional fix reaches.

The wiring is not here. It costs a second render per cue on a path that touches
every frame, and the test above is what it has to prove itself against.

entry.title: docs: derive the canonical URL from Read the Docs' published base
entry.content:
docs: derive the canonical URL from Read the Docs' published base

`site_url` was the bare host root, but RTD serves every page under a version
prefix. So each nested page declared a canonical one path segment short of
anything RTD serves: `/start/install/` returns 404 while the page itself lives
at `/en/latest/start/install/`. Search engines are entitled to drop or mis-rank
a page whose canonical does not resolve.

RTD publishes the correct base per build in READTHEDOCS_CANONICAL_URL. The
fallback keeps a local `poe docs` build deterministic when that variable is
absent, and carries a version prefix so the local build and the published one
agree about the shape of a canonical.

`poe docs-canonical` pins both failure modes, since neither is visible in a
built page without fetching the URL: a base at the host root, and a base with no
trailing slash — `urljoin` drops the last segment of that one, so a
version-looking base silently canonicalises without its version.

entry.title: fix(subtitles): key the run-path cache and picker picks by profile la…
entry.content:
fix(subtitles): key the run-path cache and picker picks by profile language

Two paths kept writing or reading the unmarked (Japanese) cache slot after
TsukiHime stopped being Japanese-only, each reopening the cross-profile hijack
the language-keyed slot was added to close.

`launch.run._configured_subtitles` gated the cache read on "some provider serves
this language" and then read the slot with no language. That gate was sufficient
only while every provider was Japanese-only; widening TsukiHime made it true for
every language, so a French run was served the Japanese file a prior run had
cached. Nothing covered `_configured_subtitles`, so the gap was invisible.

The picker stored a pick under the attachment's own tag. For an untagged
attachment — the case the boundary deliberately lets through — that resolved to
the Japanese slot, orphaning the hand pick for the profile that made it and
serving it to a Japanese one. Picks are keyed by the profile that chose them;
the boundary has already established the pick belongs to it.

Also: the picker's mixed-language test compared display names, so one language
spelled two ways (fr/fra) labelled every row; it compares language bases now.
A test comment claimed `fra` as a negative control for `fr` when it is a valid
alias that matches — the case is now present and asserts what it does.

entry.title: feat(subtitles): serve every language TsukiHime carries, keyed by pro…
entry.content:
feat(subtitles): serve every language TsukiHime carries, keyed by profile

The provider dropped every non-Japanese attachment while parsing a release
(`_is_japanese` in `_attachment_from_raw`). A census of 30 releases found 30+
languages, with French attachments outnumbering Japanese ones — so the filter
discarded most of what the source serves, and "TsukiHime as a French source"
was a filter to delete rather than an adapter to write.

Language becomes part of the provider contract: candidates carry their raw
reported tag, `ProviderContext` carries the profile's target, and the boundary
applies the existing `lang_matches` policy to a non-blank tag. An untagged
result is not auto-attached — it reaches the manual picker instead, since a
human can judge what a missing tag cannot.

Three things had to move with it:

- The filter runs before `fetch`'s uniqueness guard. A release holds one
  subtitle per language, so counting all of them made every real multilingual
  release ambiguous.
- The cache slot gains a language. It was keyed on (video, title, episode,
  size, mode), so a French session could be served the Japanese file a previous
  session stored; the jp-only capability had been the accidental guard.
  Japanese keeps the unmarked legacy spelling, so existing hand-picked `-raw`
  and `-retimed` entries stay addressable.
- `ProviderContext.language` defaults to the target rather than to None, which
  means "do not filter" — the wrong default for an unattended fetch.

`fetch_provider_path` takes the context whole instead of unpacking seven
keywords and repacking them one line later.
